title: Preservation through records and a specialized audience
summary: Perhanis says consciously articulating the form can preserve it. Rose says a form never dies but no one now needs it, and that he listens to records.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well, I want to ask you this, Al, because this gets to something that I think is indicative of where the traditional style may be or the New Orleans style may be right now or the form. Is that don't you believe that one of the compensations for historical change, and in this case probably an historical change that threatens the music itself, is also, at the same time, something that helps to preserve it. That is, that as you get a historical perspective on a time and a musical form, you begin to become conscious of it, just like I think that you're an example of someone who's consciously articulating the form and style, and you're going to write something about it, and other people are writing things about it or other things, and they're consciously articulating it. Now, by consciously articulating this as a form, because certainly the musicians don't do it and have not done it, and they shouldn't have to, you're in a sense making it recognizable. So that, let's say, 20 years from now, someone who was born maybe even outside the United States could consciously create a jazz band, by not even have, not have, you know, been as foreign to the circumstances of jazz as you've been, it could be, where you've grown up with it and you grew into it, and this would be something like, it's not quite like a manual, how to form a jazz band, but it's approaching that kind of thing, where if someone wants to do it, they can do it, and in that sense, the form is not extinct.
Well, in that sense, of course, no form ever dies, it always exists, except for the fact that nobody uses it.

And I would say that the likelihood of it being used in the future can't be predicted, but I would say that there would be little likelihood because of the fact that it no longer meets, as far as I can see, the psychological and emotional demands of the population. Now, it may be that society will sometimes swing to the kinds of attitudes that produced it, but I certainly don't see it reflected in any of the society of the world that I know.

Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Well, this, I guess that my attitude is that it is preserved, albeit in a particular form, that is, it's conscious among a certain amount of critics and record collectors and, let's say, a specialized audience.

That is, what it has, it's moved from an undifferentiated audience of a total lifestyle, a total way of life, to a specialized audience within the total culture, so that jazz now becomes something that's of interest to a jazz fan or a jazz enthusiast or a record collector or this and that.

Now, you kind of skirt, your life sort of skirts through, through, weaves in and out of all those things. That is, you knew it at a time when it was unspecialized and it was just a way of life and you were part of that way of life and you've lived through a history which seen it become kind of a little pocket in the culture. Exactly.
Where it's become kind of a specialized interest. That's right.
Right. Now, the only, the only note of optimism that I could lend to this business about the extinction of the style would be that it is preserved.

My interest in it is not purely an intellectual interest, believe me. And I, this is my first visit to New Orleans. So there's no way that I could have absorbed it when I was growing up. But I listened to records.
And all I can say is thank goodness that these records were preserved and made available to me. You know, because there would be absolutely no way.
Well, that's where my jazz is too. That's when I, when I want to hear jazz, I play records. Yeah. Of course. But I don't look for it in live performance anymore.
